SHIPPED · 2026

The Receipts, One Year Later

7 October 2026·3 min read·649 words

Published 7 October 2026. This is the text that ran on Medium, set here.

On this page

  • I. The Last Word I Said
  • II. What I Actually Did
  • III. The Part I Am Actually Proud Of
  • IV. What Is Not Built
  • V. On Being Called High-Risk
  • VI. Why I Am Talking Again

I went quiet for eleven months.

Not blocked. Not burnt out. Not silenced. I stopped talking — because in October 2025 I was a fourteen-year-old writing manifestos about a company that did not yet exist, and I had nothing to show anyone except adjectives.

I am not interested in adjectives. So I went and built the thing.

I. The Last Word I Said

In The Architecture of Ambition I told an algorithm that had run my life as a case study that "every time you generate a report about me, you're confirming that I'm already in your system."

I was fourteen. It was the most confident sentence I had ever written, and I could not point to a single line of code that proved it.

So I left.

II. What I Actually Did

Not a roadmap. Not a pitch deck. A test suite that runs.

  • 18 tests. All of them passing. Every one a receipt, not a claim. Clone BradDevicesOfficial/BradVector and run them yourself.
  • 84 reference documents, 17,693 lines of specification, cross-linked and self-consistent.
  • 1,738 lines — the unified specification, merged into one book with a table of contents.
  • Every commit verified before it landed, by CI that refuses to publish otherwise.

I built an assembler. An interpreter. A debugger. A cycle-level profiler. A reference driver layer. A mathematics library with neural kernels, tested to exact floating-point values — 0.84580 want 0.84580, not "approximately correct."

III. The Part I Am Actually Proud Of

On the fifth of October 2026 I cut a tagged release: v0.1.0.

Three architectures — linux-x86_64, linux-aarch64, macos-arm64. Nine artifacts. Every one shipped with a SHA-256 checksum, and I verified the checksum myself before writing this sentence. You can check me: the release page lists every hash.

Then I downloaded my own release on a machine I did not build it on, checked the hash, ran the binary, and it reported:

BradDev Kit v0.1.0 (reference)
all checks PASSED

A downloadable binary and a passing test run are the same event. The release job is designed to refuse to publish if the suite is red.

That is the whole company in miniature: the receipt is the product.

IV. What Is Not Built

I am not a hardware company yet. I will not pretend otherwise.

No Brad Devices silicon has been fabricated. No processor of mine exists in metal. I have no foundry, no fabrication partner, and no price to quote you. The instruction sets are DESIGNED. The toolchain SHIPPED. The difference is not a nuance — it is the entire difference.

Anyone selling you a "chip startup" at fifteen is selling you a mood board. I am selling you a test suite and a checksum.

V. On Being Called High-Risk

The assessment was not wrong. It was incomplete.

I am fifteen, in Kisumu, and I am building silicon — the one category the West does not expect from here, because it has quietly decided that Africa arrives with fintech and agritech. Those are the doors left open.

Fine. I am walking through a different one.

Thick skin is not a personality trait. It is infrastructure. You build it because the alternative is calibrating your ambition to whatever the last person was comfortable with.

VI. Why I Am Talking Again

Because there is finally something to hand you.

Not a vision. Not a manifesto.

  • A repository you can clone — BradDevicesOfficial/BradVector, MIT licensed.
  • A release you can download — v0.1.0, three architectures, nine artifacts.
  • A site with the specification in public — brad-devices.vercel.app.

The hash is in the release notes. The binary is yours to rebuild. Nothing above requires trusting me, which is the entire point.

I said in October 2025 that I was building BradVerse. It is now Brad Devices, and it is a company, and it ships.

The architecture is sound. The execution has caught up.

— The Architect Kisumu, Kenya
